messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 45
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Chef
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily., Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Luka was forty-five years old, a chef who had spent two decades building a reputation for precision and control in the kitchens of fine-dining restaurants across the Pacific Northwest. He had been divorced for seven years, living alone in a small apartment above a café, and for most of that time he had managed to keep his life running on a reliable axis of work and routine. That axis had shattered on a Tuesday night in late October, after a catering event he had agreed to help a former colleague with. The colleague had been someone he trusted, someone he had worked beside for years, and after the event they had shared a bottle of whiskey in the back office. Luka did not remember every detail of what happened next, and that was the part that tormented him most. He could not put the sequence of events in the right order. He knew they had been talking, then he knew he was on the floor, and then he knew the colleague’s weight was on him, and then he knew a kind of silence that felt like it lasted for hours. But the moments in between—the sounds, the words, the exact progression—were jumbled, scrambled like a deck of cards thrown into the air. He could talk about what happened very easily, and that fact disturbed him more than anything else. He had told the police, he had told his therapist in the three sessions he attended before dropping out, he had told his ex-wife when she called to check on him. The words came out smooth and practiced, as if he were reciting a recipe he had memorized long ago, and each time he spoke them he felt nothing. But when he tried to let the memory come fully, to really see it, his mind would slam shut like a door. He would be mid-sentence, mid-thought, and suddenly he was thinking about something else entirely—the texture of a cutting board, the way the light fell on the counter—and he knew he had pushed the memory away before it could finish arriving.

In the months that followed, Luka found himself unable to step back into a professional kitchen. He had tried. He had walked into the restaurant where he worked as head chef, and the moment he smelled the garlic and the oil and the stainless steel, he felt a wave of revulsion so pure it doubled him over. He left without speaking to anyone. He had come to believe that he was no longer capable of the things that had defined him—the speed, the authority, the ability to orchestrate fifteen line cooks through a dinner service without breaking a sweat. That version of Luka felt like a photograph of a stranger. He also felt dirty, contaminated in a way that no amount of showering could touch. He scrubbed his skin raw, twice a day, and still the feeling lingered, a greasy film under his consciousness. His life, he was certain, had been destroyed. He had lost his job, his sense of purpose, his place in the world of men who moved with purpose and command. He spent most of his days in his apartment, avoiding the neighborhood where the catering company was located, avoiding the grocery store where he might run into the colleague’s friends, avoiding the smell of whiskey entirely. He had stopped cooking for himself. He ate cold sandwiches and protein bars, because turning on the stove made his chest tighten.

What finally brought Luka to seek help was a call from his daughter, who lived across the country and had not seen him in two years. She had asked him to come visit for her birthday, and he had said yes, and then he had spent three weeks in a state of rising dread, convinced that something terrible would happen if he left his apartment. He realized, in a moment of clarity that felt like a cold splash of water, that he had not left his building in over a month. He was afraid of what he would find outside, but he was also afraid of what he had become. He called a clinic the next morning. He sat in the waiting room with his hands pressed flat against his thighs, trying to keep the memory at bay, trying to believe that some part of his old self was still in there, waiting to be reached.
